literature.headline_zh: 人偏肺病毒本期文献呈现多方向研究进展
literature.lead_zh: 本期人偏肺病毒研究集中呈现以下进展。
key_findings_zh: 多级精密筛选将 CMNPD3066、CMNPD12667、CMNPD25748、SPECS-AE-765 和 SPECS-AP-123 确定为计算优先级最高的化合物。 [10.1080/1062936x.2026.2734388]
人偏肺病毒在住院儿童中的检出率为6.06%,2025年出现了非典型的春季高峰,3月阳性率最高达36.84%。3-6岁儿童感染率最高,且疫情后阳性率在女性中更高(P. [10.21203/rs.3.rs-10541131/v1]

papers.title: Structural insights into the binding potential of natural therapeutic leads as antiviral agents against human Metapneumovirus nucleoprotein
papers.abstract: Human metapneumovirus (hMPV), a member of the family Pneumoviridae and the genus Metapneumovirus, is a prevalent cause of respiratory tract infections, leading to severe complications and even death. As of now, there are no approved specific antiviral drugs or vaccines for hMPV, underscoring the need for potential therapeutic candidates. Hence, the present study employed a structure-based virtual screening (SBVS) of prepared ligands from CMNPD and SPECS databases against the hMPV nucleoprotein. Multi-level precision screening identified CMNPD3066, CMNPD12667, CMNPD25748, SPECS-AE-765, and SPECS-AP-123 as the top computationally prioritized compounds. These compounds demonstrated favourable predicted interactions with the docking scores ranging from -9.8 to -7.5 kcal/mol, and post-docking MMGBSA binding free energies ranging from -74.02 to -54.81 kcal/mol. Further, ADME/T evaluation predicted that these candidates were not involved in the violation of Lipinski's rule of five (Ro5) and all demonstrated favourable pharmacokinetic profiles. Subsequent 500 ns molecular dynamics simulations (MDS) and essential dynamics (ED) analyses, including principal component analysis (PCA) and free energy landscape (FEL) mapping, revealed the conformational stability of the nucleoprotein-ligand complexes throughout the simulation period. Collectively, the study concludes that the identified hit molecules are promising binding candidates for therapeutic development against hMPV and warrant further experimental and clinical validation.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to identify potential antiviral agents against human metapneumovirus (hMPV) by employing structure-based virtual screening of ligands from CMNPD and SPECS databases against the hMPV nucleoprotein. The research highlights the need for specific therapeutic candidates due to the lack of approved antiviral drugs or vaccines for hMPV. The study identified five compounds as top computational leads, which showed favorable predicted interactions with docking scores ranging from -9.8 to -7.5 kcal/mol and binding free energies from -74.02 to -54.81 kcal/mol. ADME/T evaluation suggested these compounds adhered to Lipinski's rule of five and had favorable pharmacokinetic profiles. Molecular dynamics simulations confirmed the conformational stability of the nucleoprotein-ligand complexes. The findings suggest these compounds are promising candidates for therapeutic development against hMPV, warranting further experimental and clinical validation. The study's results are based on computational methods, which may have limitations in real-world applicability.

papers.title: Cardiac Complications of Infections Due to Respiratory Syncytial Virus and Human Metapneumovirus: A Systematic Review and Pooled Analysis of Clinical Features
papers.abstract: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and human metapneumovirus (hMPV) are major causes of respiratory tract infections across different age groups. Although primarily regarded as respiratory pathogens, both viruses have been associated with cardiac complications, whose clinical spectrum remains incompletely characterized. We systematically reviewed published cases of RSV- and hMPV-associated cardiac involvement and compared their clinical characteristics and outcomes. PubMed, Scopus, and EMBASE were systematically searched for reports describing cardiac complications associated with laboratory-confirmed RSV or hMPV infection. Individual patient data were pooled and analyzed using descriptive and univariate analyses. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify characteristics associated with hMPV versus RSV diagnosis, while multiple correspondence analysis (MCA) was performed to explore multivariate patterns of clinical presentation. Age-stratified sensitivity analyses were additionally performed. analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on human metapneumovirus (hMPV) infection and disease, specifically examining cardiac complications associated with hMPV. The central question is to compare the clinical characteristics and outcomes of hMPV-related cardiac involvement with those of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review systematically searched PubMed, Scopus, and EMBASE for reports describing cardiac complications linked to laboratory-confirmed RSV or hMPV infection. The included studies were analyzed using descriptive and univariate methods, with multivariable logistic regression and multiple correspondence analysis (MCA) employed to identify associations and patterns of clinical presentation. Age-stratified sensitivity analyses were also conducted.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review included 102 cases, with 31 hMPV cases (30.4%) and 71 RSV cases (69.6%). hMPV cases were significantly older than RSV cases (41.5 years, interquartile range 3.5–63.0 vs. 1.5 years, interquartile range 0.2–31.0; p < 0.001). The study highlights the need for further research to characterize the clinical spectrum of cardiac complications associated with hMPV.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review notes that the clinical spectrum of cardiac complications associated with hMPV remains incompletely characterized. There is a lack of detailed information on the mechanisms underlying these complications and the potential differences in outcomes between hMPV and RSV infections.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The findings suggest that further research is needed to better understand the clinical features and outcomes of hMPV-associated cardiac complications. This includes studies that explore the mechanisms of cardiac involvement and the development of targeted diagnostic and therapeutic strategies.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review and pooled analysis investigates cardiac complications associated with human metapneumovirus (hMPV) infection, comparing them with those of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). The review included 102 cases, with 31 hMPV cases and 71 RSV cases. hMPV cases were significantly older than RSV cases, indicating potential differences in clinical presentation. The study highlights the incomplete characterization of hMPV-related cardiac complications and underscores the need for further research to clarify mechanisms and improve diagnostic and therapeutic approaches. The findings emphasize the importance of understanding the distinct clinical profiles of these viruses to enhance patient care and public health strategies.

papers.title: High Conservation of the Human Metapneumovirus Fusion Protein in Contemporary Global Sequences Supports Its Continued Relevance for Therapeutic and Prophylactic Consideration
papers.abstract: Human metapneumovirus (hMPV) is associated with severe disease in young children, older adults, and medically high-risk individuals. The hMPV F protein is highly immunogenic and a well-established target of neutralizing antibodies. In-depth hMPV surveillance data remain limited and may provide valuable insight into therapeutic development. Here we assembled a contemporary dataset of F gene sequences acquired from hMPV-positive nasal swab specimens collected between 2022 and 2023, together with contemporary F gene sequences from public surveillance databases, collected between 2017 and 2025. All sequences were subtyped and evaluated for residue-level similarity to reference alleles. Of 724 sequences in the combined contemporary dataset, A2 was the most predominant subtype accounting for nearly half of all sequences (50.83%). The mean F gene sequence similarity to reference alleles was 99.90%, 99.95%, and 99.84% for A2, B1, and B2, respectively; the least conserved residues were the stalk residue 518 for A2 (88.52% similarity to reference allele); BinD residue 450 for B1 (96.60% similarity); and site III residue 36 for B2 (77.88% similarity). Structural analysis showed that observed mutations were predominantly surface-exposed, with no evidence of novel N-linked glycosylation sequons, and were not predicted to significantly alter F protein structure. Overall, these findings indicate that the F protein is highly conserved across subtypes, with sequence variation unlikely to result in meaningful structural differences, thereby supporting development of F-targeted therapeutics against hMPV infection.

papers.title_zh: 人偏肺病毒 融合蛋白在当代全球序列中的高度保守性支持其与治疗和预防考虑的持续相关性
papers.source_body_en: Human metapneumovirus (hMPV) is associated with severe disease in young children, older adults, and medically high-risk individuals. The hMPV F protein is highly immunogenic and a well-established target of neutralizing antibodies. In-depth hMPV surveillance data remain limited and may provide valuable insight into therapeutic development. Here we assembled a contemporary dataset of F gene sequences acquired from hMPV-positive nasal swab specimens collected between 2022 and 2023, together with contemporary F gene sequences from public surveillance databases, collected between 2017 and 2025. All sequences were subtyped and evaluated for residue-level similarity to reference alleles. Of 724 sequences in the combined contemporary dataset, A2 was the most predominant subtype accounting for nearly half of all sequences (50.83%). The mean F gene sequence similarity to reference alleles was 99.90%, 99.95%, and 99.84% for A2, B1, and B2, respectively; the least conserved residues were the stalk residue 518 for A2 (88.52% similarity to reference allele); BinD residue 450 for B1 (96.60% similarity); and site III residue 36 for B2 (77.88% similarity). Structural analysis showed that observed mutations were predominantly surface-exposed, with no evidence of novel N-linked glycosylation sequons, and were not predicted to significantly alter F protein structure. Overall, these findings indicate that the F protein is highly conserved across subtypes, with sequence variation unlikely to result in meaningful structural differences, thereby supporting development of F-targeted therapeutics against hMPV infection.

papers.title: Emerging Trends in the Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Management of Human Metapneumovirus-Associated Respiratory Infections
papers.abstract: Introduction: Human Metapneumovirus is a significant respiratory pathogen causing infections across all age groups, particularly in young children, immunocompromised individuals, and the elderly. Despite its clinical relevance, there are currently no approved vaccines or specific antiviral treatments for Human Metapneumovirus, necessitating further research into therapeutic and preventive strategies. Methods: A systematic literature review was conducted using peer-reviewed journals, clinical trials, and recent studies focusing on Human Metapneumovirus infection. Data were extracted and analyzed to evaluate the effectiveness of antiviral therapies, monoclonal antibodies, immunomodulators, and vaccine candidates. Results: Studies indicate that Human Metapneumovirus primarily targets the respiratory epithelium, triggering immune responses that contribute to both viral clearance and disease pathogenesis. Investigational therapies, including fusion inhibitors and protease inhibitors, show promise but require further validation. Immunomodulatory agents and herbal remedies may offer supportive benefits, but their efficacy against Human Metapneumovirus remains unproven. Advances in vaccine development are ongoing, with several candidates in preclinical and early clinical stages. Discussion: HMPV continues to pose a substantial public health burden due to its seasonal outbreaks, clinical similarity to other respiratory viruses, and absence of specific therapies. The virus evades immune responses via multiple mechanisms, contributing to disease severity, particularly in vulnerable populations. Although supportive care is currently the mainstay, emerging antivirals and vaccines may offer future solutions. Improved diagnostic access, public awareness, and targeted research are essential for controlling HMPV infections. Conclusion: Human Metapneumovirus continues to pose a public health challenge due to the lack of targeted treatments and vaccines. Ongoing research into antiviral agents, monoclonal antibodies, and vaccines is critical for effective disease management. Further clinical trials are needed to establish safe and effective therapeutic options.

source_records.abstract: Introduction: Human Metapneumovirus is a significant respiratory pathogen causing infections across all age groups, particularly in young children, immunocompromised individuals, and the elderly. Despite its clinical relevance, there are currently no approved vaccines or specific antiviral treatments for Human Metapneumovirus, necessitating further research into therapeutic and preventive strategies. Methods: A systematic literature review was conducted using peer-reviewed journals, clinical trials, and recent studies focusing on Human Metapneumovirus infection. Data were extracted and analyzed to evaluate the effectiveness of antiviral therapies, monoclonal antibodies, immunomodulators, and vaccine candidates. Results: Studies indicate that Human Metapneumovirus primarily targets the respiratory epithelium, triggering immune responses that contribute to both viral clearance and disease pathogenesis. Investigational therapies, including fusion inhibitors and protease inhibitors, show promise but require further validation. Immunomodulatory agents and herbal remedies may offer supportive benefits, but their efficacy against Human Metapneumovirus remains unproven. Advances in vaccine development are ongoing, with several candidates in preclinical and early clinical stages. Although supportive care is currently the mainstay, emerging antivirals and vaccines may offer future solutions. Improved diagnostic access, public awareness, and targeted research are essential for controlling HMPV infections. Conclusion: Human Metapneumovirus continues to pose a public health challenge due to the lack of targeted treatments and vaccines. papers.abstract_zh: 引言:人偏肺病毒(HMPV)是一种重要的呼吸道病原体,可在不同年龄段人群中引发感染,尤其是在幼儿、免疫功能低下者及老年人中。尽管其具有重要的临床意义,但目前尚无获批的抗病毒药物或针对人偏肺病毒的特异性治疗方法,亟需进一步研究治疗和预防策略。方法:通过系统性文献综述,检索同行评议期刊、临床试验及近期研究,重点关注人偏肺病毒感染。提取并分析数据,以评估抗病毒药物、单克隆抗体、免疫调节剂及疫苗候选物的有效性。结果:研究表明,人偏肺病毒主要靶向呼吸道上皮细胞,触发免疫应答,这些免疫应答既有助于病毒清除,也会导致疾病发病机制。正在研发的治疗方法,包括融合抑制剂和蛋白酶抑制剂,显示出潜力,但仍需进一步验证。免疫调节剂和中草药可能提供支持性益处,但其对人偏肺病毒的有效性尚未得到证实。疫苗研发取得进展,多个候选疫苗已进入临床前及早期临床阶段。讨论:由于人偏肺病毒的季节性流行、与其他呼吸道病毒的临床相似性以及缺乏特异性治疗方法,该病毒继续对公共卫生构成重大负担。该病毒通过多种机制逃避免疫应答,导致疾病严重程度增加,尤其是在易感人群中。尽管目前主要采用支持性治疗,但新兴的抗病毒药物和疫苗可能为未来提供解决方案。改善诊断可及性、提高公众意识及开展针对性研究对于控制人偏肺病毒感染至关重要。结论:由于缺乏针对性治疗方法和疫苗,人偏肺病毒继续对公共卫生构成挑战。针对抗病毒药物、单克隆抗体及疫苗的持续研究对于有效疾病管理至关重要。亟需进一步临床试验以确立安全有效的治疗方案。

papers.title: Multimodal reasoning for broadly neutralizing antibody discovery from label-free human B cell repertoires across virus families
papers.abstract: Discovering broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) from human natural immune repertoires remains a fundamental challenge in immunology, hindered by: the extreme rarity of bnAb, incomplete understanding of their cellular origins across pathogens, and the inability of existing computational tools to generalize across emerging viral threats. Here we present ImmuneAgent, a closed-loop AI system that integrates multimodal reasoning with continual meta-learning and wet-lab feedback to overcome these barriers. Applied to screen the natural BCR repertoires from vaccinated or infected cohorts, the system achieves a ~55% neutralization antibody discovery rate (60 of 110 cloned candidates) and a ~11% bnAb yield (12 of 110), substantially outperforming a state-of-the-art sequence-based neutralization predictor or cofolding models evaluated at the same cloning budget. Five ImmuneAgent-discovered antibodies conferred 100% in vivo protection against lethal influenza challenge, comparable to the clinical-stage therapeutic MEDI8852. The system recovered the cellular and structural determinants of bnAb activity and identified FCRL5+CD27+ atypical memory B cells as a conserved bnAb reservoir and hydrophobic interface enrichment as a cross-viral structural signature, which generalized to unseen antigens, discovering human metapneumovirus (hMPV) cross-neutralizing and human papillomavirus (HPV)-neutralizing antibodies without antigen-specific sorting. These results validate that ImmuneAgent is a generalizable framework for rapid therapeutic antibody discovery against emerging viral threats.

papers.title_zh: 从跨病毒家族的无标记人 B 细胞库中发现广泛中和抗体的多模式推理
papers.source_body_en: Discovering broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) from human natural immune repertoires remains a fundamental challenge in immunology, hindered by: the extreme rarity of bnAb, incomplete understanding of their cellular origins across pathogens, and the inability of existing computational tools to generalize across emerging viral threats. Here we present ImmuneAgent, a closed-loop AI system that integrates multimodal reasoning with continual meta-learning and wet-lab feedback to overcome these barriers. Applied to screen the natural BCR repertoires from vaccinated or infected cohorts, the system achieves a ~55% neutralization antibody discovery rate (60 of 110 cloned candidates) and a ~11% bnAb yield (12 of 110), substantially outperforming a state-of-the-art sequence-based neutralization predictor or cofolding models evaluated at the same cloning budget. Five ImmuneAgent-discovered antibodies conferred 100% in vivo protection against lethal influenza challenge, comparable to the clinical-stage therapeutic MEDI8852. The system recovered the cellular and structural determinants of bnAb activity and identified FCRL5+CD27+ atypical memory B cells as a conserved bnAb reservoir and hydrophobic interface enrichment as a cross-viral structural signature, which generalized to unseen antigens, discovering human metapneumovirus (hMPV) cross-neutralizing and human papillomavirus (HPV)-neutralizing antibodies without antigen-specific sorting. These results validate that ImmuneAgent is a generalizable framework for rapid therapeutic antibody discovery against emerging viral threats.
papers.abstract_zh: 从人类自然免疫库中发现广泛中和抗体 (bnAb) 仍然是免疫学中的一项基本挑战,其阻碍因素包括:bnAb 极其稀有、对病原体细胞起源的不完全了解以及现有计算工具无法概括新兴病毒威胁。在这里,我们展示了 ImmuneAgent,这是一个闭环人工智能系统,它将多模态推理与持续元学习和湿实验室反馈相结合,以克服这些障碍。该系统应用于从接种疫苗或感染的 队列研究 中筛选天然 BCR 库,实现了约 55% 的中和抗体发现率(110 个克隆候选者中的 60 个)和约 11% bnAb 产量(110 个克隆候选者中的 12 个),大大优于在相同克隆预算下评估的最先进的基于序列的中和预测器或共折叠模型。ImmuneAgent 发现的五种抗体可针对致命流感攻击提供 100% 体内保护,与临床阶段治疗药物 MEDI8852 相当。该系统恢复了 bnAb 活性的细胞和结构决定因素,并将 FCRL5+CD27+ 非典型记忆 B 细胞鉴定为保守的 bnAb 储存宿主,并将疏水界面富集鉴定为交叉病毒结构特征,其推广到看不见的抗原,发现 人偏肺病毒 (hMPV) 交叉中和和人乳头瘤病毒 (HPV) 中和抗体,无需抗原特异性分选。这些结果验证了 ImmuneAgent 是一个通用框架,可用于快速发现新出现的病毒威胁的治疗性抗体。

papers.full_text: AbstractBackgroundThe detection of Aspergillus in the lower respiratory tract complicates the clinical course of viral pneumonia and is linked to poor outcomes, but prior evidence is confined to the intensive care unit (ICU) or single-virus settings (e.g., influenza or SARS-CoV-2). Whether its frequency and prognostic significance differ across viral etiologies in hospitalized adults remains unknown.MethodsThis multicenter retrospective cohort study included adults with community-acquired viral pneumonia at seven tertiary hospitals in China (2017-2025). Patients were categorized into SARS-CoV-2, influenza, or other viral groups. The exposure was lower respiratory tract Aspergillus detection (via using culture, real-time PCR, or metagenomic next-generation sequencing). The primary outcome was in-hospital all-cause mortality.ResultsAmong 929 patients, Aspergillus was detected in 175 (18.8%). The detection rates differed significantly across viral etiologies (33.2% in patients with influenza, 14.6% in those with SARS-CoV-2, and 7.4% in those with other viruses; P < 0.001). In the fully adjusted model, Aspergillus detection was independently associated with increased overall mortality (aOR = 2.99; 95% CI 1.60–5.58; P < 0.001), but the association varied markedly by viral etiology. Virus-stratified analyses revealed that in influenza, Aspergillus detection remained independently associated with mortality after multivariable adjustment, and the association was consistently observed across prespecified subgroups, including non-ventilated patients, whereas in SARS-CoV-2, the association was largely confined to ventilated patients.ConclusionLower respiratory tract Aspergillus detection differed substantially by viral etiology and was most frequent in patients with influenza pneumonia. It was independently associated with increased mortality across all influenza subgroups, including non-ventilated patients, whereas in SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia this association was largely confined to mechanical ventilation patients. These findings support a virus-stratified approach to fungal surveillance and warrant prospective validation.Keywords: Aspergillus, cohort study, influenza, mortality, SARS-CoV-2, viral pneumonia 2.Materials and methods2.1.Ethics approvalThe study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of Shijiazhuang People’s Hospital (Approval No. 2026090) and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Given the retrospective design and use of anonymized data, the Ethics Committee waived the requirement for informed consent.2.2.Study participantsWe included patients admitted to seven tertiary hospitals in China with viral pneumonia between February 1, 2017, and April 1, 2025, reported as per STROBE guidelines (von Elm et al., 2007).Inclusion criteria: (1) diagnosis of community-acquired pneumonia using standard criteria (clinical signs and symptoms plus radiographic evidence of alveolar inflammation, per the 2025 ATS guideline (Jones et al., 2026); (2) laboratory confirmation of viral infection. This confirmation required either a positive result for viral pathogens (including SARS-CoV-2, influenza A/B, adenovirus, herpes simplex virus, rhinovirus, parainfluenza, human coronavirus, respiratory syncytial virus, cytomegalovirus, coxsackievirus, human metapneumovirus, and varicella-zoster virus) via real-time PCR or metagenomic next-generation sequencing of respiratory specimens (sputum, tracheal aspirates, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, or nasopharyngeal swabs), or a positive rapid antigen test for SARS-CoV-2 or influenza.Patients were excluded if they met any of the following criteria: hospitalization within 30 days prior to admission; pulmonary fungal infection within 3 months prior to admission; pulmonary embolism; NYHA class III-IV heart failure; active tuberculosis or nontuberculous mycobacterial infection; HIV infection; pregnancy or lactation; or mixed viral infection.2.3.Data collectionClinical data were systematically extracted from the electronic medical records of all seven participating centers and entered into a standardized case report form via the Free Electronic Data Capture system (version 2.0; Beijing Free Clinical Medical Technology Co., Ltd., Beijing, China). Data extraction was performed independently by two trained clinical research coordinators at each site. Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion or by adjudication from the principal investigator.The following data domains were collected for each patient: (1) Demographic and baseline characteristics, including age, sex, and smoking history; (2) Comorbidities, including: hypertension, diabetes mellitus, coronary heart disease (CHD), cerebrovascular disease, chronic lung disease (asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or diffuse interstitial lung disease), chronic kidney disease (CKD) (with or without dialysis), chronic liver disease (hepatitis, cirrhosis, or liver failure), and immunosuppression (attributable to underlying autoimmune disease, long-term immunosuppressive medication, or active malignancy); (3) Vital signs at hospital admission, including: maximum body temperature (Tmax), pulse rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, and respiratory rate; (4) Laboratory parameters obtained within 24 h of admission, including: complete blood count [white blood cell (WBC) count, neutrophil (NEU) count, lymphocyte (LYM) count, monocyte count, hemoglobin (HGB), and platelet (PLT) count], liver function tests (alanine aminotransferase; aspartate aminotransferase and lactate dehydrogenase), creatine kinase, serum albumin (ALB), serum creatinine, prothrombin time, D-dimer, C-reactive protein (CRP), and procalcitonin (PCT); and arterial blood gas analysis (pH, arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide, arterial partial pressure of oxygen, oxygenation index [arterial partial pressure of oxygen/fraction of inspired oxygen], and lactic acid (Lac)]; (5) Microbiological data, specifically: the results of Aspergillus detection in lower respiratory tract samples (sputum, tracheal aspirate, or bronchoalveolar lavage fluid) via fungal culture, real-time PCR, or metagenomic next-generation sequencing. Sputum specimens were subjected to cytological quality screening prior to processing; eligibility was defined as fewer than 10 squamous epithelial cells and more than 25 leukocytes per low-power field. (6) Treatment data, including antiviral, antibacterial, and antifungal therapies, systemic glucocorticoid use, and invasive mechanical ventilation; and (7) clinical outcomes, specifically in-hospital all-cause mortality, and 28-day in-hospital mortality was also assessed as a secondary outcome.2.4.Statistical analysisStatistical analyses were performed using R version 3.6.3 and Free Statistics version 2.2. Missing laboratory and clinical values (e.g., D-dimer, albumin) were imputed using multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE; 20 imputed datasets); the proportions of missing data are summarized in Supplementary Table S1. Continuous variables are presented as means ± standard deviations (SD) or medians with interquartile ranges (IQR), and were compared using analysis of variance (ANOVA) or the Kruskal-Wallis test, as appropriate. Categorical variables are expressed as frequencies (percentages) and were compared using the Pearson χ2 or Fisher’s exact test. Univariate logistic regression models were used to estimate odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for Aspergillus detection and in-hospital mortality. Variables with P < 0.05 in the univariate analysis, alongside clinically relevant confounders, were incorporated into sequentially built multivariable models: Model 1 adjusted for demographics (age, sex, and smoking status); Model 2 further adjusted for inflammatory markers and laboratory findings; Model 3 additionally included comorbidities; and Model 4 (the full model) further incorporated antiviral and antibacterial therapies, systemic glucocorticoids, as well as mechanical ventilation. Pre-specified stratified analyses were performed to assess effect modification by age (<60 vs. ≥60 years), sex, presence of comorbidities, and mechanical ventilation in the overall cohort. In addition, we conducted subgroup analyses within the influenza and SARS-CoV-2 subgroups to assess the moderating effects of age, sex, and mechanical ventilation on the effect. Interactions were assessed by including multiplicative interaction terms in the logistic regression models, and statistical significance was determined by likelihood ratio tests. A two-sided P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Patients in the SARS-CoV-2 group were the oldest (75.6 ± 11.5 years), and had the longest hospital stay (25.5 ± 9.9 days). This group also exhibited the highest prevalences of hypertension, CHD, and cerebrovascular disease, alongside the lowest ALB and LYM counts, and the highest rate of glucocorticoid use (66.3%). Conversely, chronic lung disease was most common in the influenza group (29.6%), which also demonstrated the highest D-dimer levels and the highest frequencies of antiviral (75.2%) and antifungal (36.0%) therapies. full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionIn this multicenter cohort of 929 hospitalized patients with viral pneumonia, Aspergillus detection in the lower respiratory tract differed significantly by viral etiology, being highest in influenza (33.2%), intermediate in SARS-CoV-2 (14.6%), and lowest in other viral pneumonias (7.4%). Aspergillus detection was independently associated with a substantially increased risk of all-cause mortality, although this association varied by virus type and was most pronounced in influenza. Subgroup analysis further indicated that, in influenza pneumonia, this association remained robust across different genders, age groups, and ventilatory statuses; whereas in SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia, the impact of Aspergillus detection on prognosis was primarily observed in male patients, elderly patients, and those requiring mechanical ventilation, with ventilatory status showing a significant interaction (interaction P-value < 0.001).Reported rates of viral pneumonia-associated Aspergillus vary widely across studies, reflecting differences in setting, case definitions, and diagnostic sensitivity rather than a single true prevalence. The pooled prevalence of IAPA in ICU patients is approximately 19.2% (range 6.4%–62.2%) (Lu et al., 2024). Similarly, the pooled prevalence of CAPA is highly heterogeneous, reported at 11.1% in ICU observational studies (Feys et al., 2021) and 17.5% in a subsequent meta-analysis (range, 2.5%–47.2%) (Gioia et al., 2024). Importantly, the burden is not confined to the ICU. CAPA has been reported in 15.7% of sub-ICU patients (Iacovelli et al., 2024) and 3.8% of inpatients during the Omicron wave (associated with a 43.5% mortality rate) (Wang et al., 2024). Furthermore, pulmonary aspergillosis occurs in 5%–33% of selected immunocompromised cohorts following other non-influenza viral infections (e.g., RSV, parainfluenza, and adenovirus) (Apostolopoulou et al., 2021).Unlike previous studies that confined their cohorts to ICU patients or those meeting strict ECMM/ISHAM consensus criteria (Verweij et al., 2020; Koehler et al., 2021), we enrolled a broader spectrum of hospitalized adults. As a result, our endpoint captures clinically meaningful airway carriage, rather than focusing solely on adjudicated IPA. To our knowledge, no prior study has compared lower respiratory tract Aspergillus detection across influenza, SARS-CoV-2, and other viral pneumonias within a single cohort. Previously, the largest comparative study was confined to intubated ICU patients (Rouzé et al., 2022), while another prospective study was limited to 140 critically ill patients (Ali et al., 2022). Furthermore, other analyses examined non-influenza viruses exclusively in highly selected transplant or hematologic populations (Magira et al., 2019; Apostolopoulou et al., 2021). Therefore, this analysis provides the first integrated, virus-stratified estimate of Aspergillus positivity and its prognostic significance across the full severity spectrum of routine inpatient care.The stepwise gradient in detection likely reflects virus-specific remodeling of pulmonary antifungal immunity rather than differential environmental exposure. Influenza induces a multi-level collapse of antifungal defense that includes epithelial barrier disruption, alveolar macrophage depletion, impaired phagocytic killing, and IFN-γ-driven suppression of the Th17/IL-22 axis (Short et al., 2016; Salazar et al., 2022; Feys et al., 2024; Seldeslachts et al., 2024). In a co-infection model, genetic ablation of IFN-γ restored Th17 responses and antifungal activity, identifying IFN-γ as a promising therapeutic target (Seldeslachts et al., 2024). In contrast, SARS-CoV-2 primarily causes pulmonary endotheliitis and microthrombosis (Ackermann et al., 2020; Bonaventura et al., 2021); furthermore, the associated hyperinflammation frequently requires corticosteroid therapy, thereby driving iatrogenic immunosuppression (Horby et al., 2021; Salazar et al., 2022; Shah et al., 2023; Xiang et al., 2025). Because cytokine-mediated inflammation and microvascular thrombosis are themselves dominant lethal factors in COVID-19, the independent prognostic impact of Aspergillus is statistically diluted by stronger mortality drivers. In our cohort, 66.3% of SARS-CoV-2 patients received glucocorticoids, compared to 23.6% of influenza patients; notably, corticosteroid exposure beyond 10 days has been linked to higher CAPA risk (OR 3.17; 95% CI 1.02–9.83) and increased mortality (77.1% vs. 43.2%, P < 0.0001) (Shah et al., 2023). These factors explain why, after adjusting for glucocorticoid use and mechanical ventilation, the prognostic significance of Aspergillus detection in SARS-CoV-2 patients was no longer evident (Model 4: aOR = 2.07; 95% CI 0.77–5.55; P = 0.15), and that detection of Aspergillus was not associated with increased mortality in SARS-CoV-2 patients not receiving mechanical ventilation (OR = 0.54, P = 0.316), suggesting that in milder cases, a positive fungal test result may represent colonization or a secondary finding rather than a lethal factor. In contrast, among mechanically ventilated patients, the 100% mortality rate in the Aspergillus-positive group highlighted the exceptionally poor outcomes observed in mechanically ventilated patients with severe COVID-19 and Aspergillus detection. However, the small sample size precluded precise risk assessment. These findings suggest that Aspergillus detection in COVID-19 patients primarily reflects the intensity of treatment and disease severity, rather than a direct cause of death. In infections caused by other viruses (e.g., rhinovirus, RSV) (Sajjan et al., 2008; Pickles and DeVincenzo, 2015; Horton et al., 2025), anatomically restricted airway injury, combined with younger age, lower comorbidity burden, and lower glucocorticoid exposure (16.8%), likely preserves immune reserve, thereby limiting both Aspergillus detection and its prognostic impact.In viral-associated pulmonary aspergillosis, distinguishing colonization from invasive disease is challenging, as galactomannan testing and culture cannot reliably differentiate them in critically ill patients (Donnelly et al., 2019; Verweij et al., 2020). In a study utilizing histopathological validation, tissue invasion was confirmed in 55% of probable IAPA cases and 50% of probable CAPA cases, including one case without antemortem clinical suspicion (Vanderbeke et al., 2023). Others have argued that microbiological detection of Aspergillus in severe viral pneumonia often reflects true infection, supporting preemptive antifungal therapy in high-risk patients (Albrich and Lamoth, 2023). Our data extend these observations beyond the ICU. In this multicenter cohort encompassing multiple viral etiologies and a full spectrum of disease severity, the detection of Aspergillus in the lower respiratory tract was a strong and independent prognostic factor for mortality in influenza patients (fully aOR = 13.77; 95% CI 2.75–68.88) but not in those with other viral pneumonias. This is consistent with the rapid clinical course described for IAPA, with a median interval of only 3 days from ICU admission to diagnosis (Schauwvlieghe et al., 2018). Our subgroup analysis further corroborated this observation. Among mechanically ventilated influenza patients with Aspergillus detection, mortality reached 90.5%. This rate approaches the 90-day mortality reported for invasive tracheobronchial aspergillosis (Nyga et al., 2020). In contrast, mortality among ventilated patients without Aspergillus detection was 44.0%. These findings further validate this high-risk phenotype.By evaluating lower respiratory tract Aspergillus detection across three viral groups under a unified framework, our study identifies “influenza plus lower respiratory tract Aspergillus detection” as a distinct, high-risk phenotype with an independent mortality risk several-fold higher than that of other groups. These findings challenge a uniform, one-size-fits-all approach…
full_text_sections.conclusion: 5.ConclusionsIn this multicenter cohort, lower respiratory tract Aspergillus detection rates differed significantly by viral etiology, being highest in influenza, intermediate in SARS-CoV-2, and lowest in other viral pneumonias. Its prognostic significance also varied by viral etiology. Aspergillus detection was independently associated with in-hospital mortality in influenza pneumonia. In SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia, however, this association was attenuated after full adjustment and was primarily observed among mechanically ventilated patients. These findings support further evaluation of a virus-stratified approach to fungal surveillance and warrant prospective validation.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionViral pneumonia is a major cause of hospitalization, acute respiratory failure, and mortality in adults, particularly among older adults and those with chronic comorbidities (Jain et al., 2015; Hanage and Schaffner, 2025). Over the past decade, seasonal and pandemic influenza, SARS-CoV-2, and other viruses have collectively altered the epidemiology and clinical presentation of viral pneumonia (Chow et al., 2023; Cilloniz et al., 2025). Patients with viral pneumonia are susceptible to various secondary infections, among which fungal infections—particularly invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IPA)—have emerged as important complications (Schauwvlieghe et al., 2018; Magira et al., 2019; MaChado et al., 2021).Respiratory viruses can damage airway epithelium, impair mucociliary clearance, and disrupt innate and adaptive immunity, thereby weakening antifungal defenses (Bridges et al., 2022; Salazar et al., 2022; Nguyen et al., 2024; Seldeslachts et al., 2024; Horton et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2025). Moreover, high-dose or prolonged glucocorticoid use, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and mechanical ventilation are recognized risk factors for IPA (Montrucchio et al., 2021; Hurt et al., 2023; Terrones-Campos et al., 2026). In intensive care unit (ICU) cohorts, influenza-associated invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IAPA) has been reported in approximately 19%–29% of patients, leading to prolonged ICU stays and mortality often exceeding 45% (Chong et al., 2022; Lu et al., 2024). In contrast, COVID-19-associated pulmonary aspergillosis (CAPA) affected approximately 2%–25% of critically ill patients, with ICU mortality exceeding 50% (Prattes et al., 2022). However, most previous studies have focused on highly selected ICU populations, primarily addressing IAPA or CAPA, with small sample sizes and few systematic comparisons between viral etiologies.In real-world hospital settings, the detection of Aspergillus in the lower respiratory tract—which often represents colonization or early infection rather than confirmed IPA—is a frequent finding among patients with viral pneumonia. Notably, our previous work demonstrated that such early detection is associated with higher mortality in influenza pneumonia (Yin et al., 2023). Whether the rate of Aspergillus detection and its prognostic implications differ by viral etiology (SARS-CoV-2, influenza, or other viruses) remains unknown in real-world hospitalized populations. To address this question, we conducted a multicenter retrospective cohort study of adult inpatients with community-acquired viral pneumonia to compare Aspergillus detection rates across different viral etiologies and to evaluate whether the associated mortality risk varies depending on the causative virus. 2.1.Ethics approvalThe study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of Shijiazhuang People’s Hospital (Approval No. 2026090) and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Given the retrospective design and use of anonymized data, the Ethics Committee waived the requirement for informed consent. 2.2.Study participantsWe included patients admitted to seven tertiary hospitals in China with viral pneumonia between February 1, 2017, and April 1, 2025, reported as per STROBE guidelines (von Elm et al., 2007).Inclusion criteria: (1) diagnosis of community-acquired pneumonia using standard criteria (clinical signs and symptoms plus radiographic evidence of alveolar inflammation, per the 2025 ATS guideline (Jones et al., 2026); (2) laboratory confirmation of viral infection. This confirmation required either a positive result for viral pathogens (including SARS-CoV-2, influenza A/B, adenovirus, herpes simplex virus, rhinovirus, parainfluenza, human coronavirus, respiratory syncytial virus, cytomegalovirus, coxsackievirus, human metapneumovirus, and varicella-zoster virus) via real-time PCR or metagenomic next-generation sequencing of respiratory specimens (sputum, tracheal aspirates, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, or nasopharyngeal swabs), or a positive rapid antigen test for SARS-CoV-2 or influenza.Patients were excluded if they met any of the following criteria: hospitalization within 30 days prior to admission; pulmonary fungal infection within 3 months prior to admission; pulmonary embolism; NYHA class III-IV heart failure; active tuberculosis or nontuberculous mycobacterial infection; HIV infection; pregnancy or lactation; or mixed viral infection. 2.3.Data collectionClinical data were systematically extracted from the electronic medical records of all seven participating centers and entered into a standardized case report form via the Free Electronic Data Capture system (version 2.0; Beijing Free Clinical Medical Technology Co., Ltd., Beijing, China). Data extraction was performed independently by two trained clinical research coordinators at each site. Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion or by adjudication from the principal investigator.The following data domains were collected for each patient: (1) Demographic and baseline characteristics, including age, sex, and smoking history; (2) Comorbidities, including: hypertension, diabetes mellitus, coronary heart disease (CHD), cerebrovascular disease, chronic lung disease (asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or diffuse interstitial lung disease), chronic kidney disease (CKD) (with or without dialysis), chronic liver disease (hepatitis, cirrhosis, or liver failure), and immunosuppression (attributable to underlying autoimmune disease, long-term immunosuppressive medication, or active malignancy); (3) Vital signs at hospital admission, including: maximum body temperature (Tmax), pulse rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, and respiratory rate; (4) Laboratory parameters obtained within 24 h of admission, including: complete blood count [white blood cell (WBC) count, neutrophil (NEU) count, lymphocyte (LYM) count, monocyte count, hemoglobin (HGB), and platelet (PLT) count], liver function tests (alanine aminotransferase; aspartate aminotransferase and lactate dehydrogenase), creatine kinase, serum albumin (ALB), serum creatinine, prothrombin time, D-dimer, C-reactive protein (CRP), and procalcitonin (PCT); and arterial blood gas analysis (pH, arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide, arterial partial pressure of oxygen, oxygenation index [arterial partial pressure of oxygen/fraction of inspired oxygen], and lactic acid (Lac)]; (5) Microbiological data, specifically: the results of Aspergillus detection in lower respiratory tract samples (sputum, tracheal aspirate, or bronchoalveolar lavage fluid) via fungal culture, real-time PCR, or metagenomic next-generation sequencing. Sputum specimens were subjected to cytological quality screening prior to processing; eligibility was defined as fewer than 10 squamous epithelial cells and more than 25 leukocytes per low-power field. (6) Treatment data, including antiviral, antibacterial, and antifungal therapies, systemic glucocorticoid use, and invasive mechanical ventilation; and (7) clinical outcomes, specifically in-hospital all-cause mortality, and 28-day in-hospital mortality was also assessed as a secondary outcome. 2.4.Statistical analysisStatistical analyses were performed using R version 3.6.3 and Free Statistics version 2.2. Missing laboratory and clinical values (e.g., D-dimer, albumin) were imputed using multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE; 20 imputed datasets); the proportions of missing data are summarized in Supplementary Table S1. Continuous variables are presented as means ± standard deviations (SD) or medians with interquartile ranges (IQR), and were compared using analysis of variance (ANOVA) or the Kruskal-Wallis test, as appropriate. Categorical variables are expressed as frequencies (percentages) and were compared using the Pearson χ2 or Fisher’s exact test. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the association between Aspergillus detection in the lower respiratory tract and mortality in patients with viral pneumonias, highlighting the need to understand fungal co-infections in viral pneumonia contexts.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This retrospective multicenter cohort study included 929 hospitalized patients with viral pneumonia in China, with a focus on those with different viral etiologies, including influenza, SARS-CoV-2, and other viruses.
analysis.methods: Exposure was defined as lower respiratory tract Aspergillus detection using culture, real-time PCR, or metagenomic next-generation sequencing. Statistical analyses were conducted using R version 3.6.3 and Free Statistics version 2.2.

analysis.summary_en: This retrospective multicenter cohort study from China investigated the association between Aspergillus detection in the lower respiratory tract and mortality in patients with viral pneumonias. The study included 929 hospitalized patients with different viral etiologies, such as influenza, SARS-CoV-2, and other viruses. Aspergillus was detected in 18.8% of patients, with the highest rate in the influenza group (33.2%) and the lowest in other viruses (7.4%). In-hospital mortality was significantly higher in the SARS-CoV-2 and influenza groups compared to other virus groups. The study found that Aspergillus detection was independently associated with increased mortality, but the association varied by viral etiology, with influenza showing the strongest link. These findings highlight the importance of monitoring for Aspergillus in patients with viral pneumonia, particularly influenza, for risk assessment and clinical management. However, the study's retrospective design and potential confounding factors limit the confidence in the results.

elements_zh.methods: 暴露定义为使用培养、实时 PCR 或宏基因组下一代测序进行下呼吸道曲霉菌检测。使用 R 版本 3.6.3 和 Free Statistics 版本 2.2 进行统计分析。
elements_zh.main_results: 929 名患者中,有 175 名患者检出曲霉菌(18.8%),其中流感组检出率最高(33.2%),其次是 SARS-CoV-2(14.6%)和其他病毒(7.4%)(P < 0.001)。与其他病毒组(4.2%,P = 0.004)相比,SARS-CoV-2 组(17.5%)和流感组(16.8%)的住院 死亡率 显着较高。

analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The study found that Aspergillus detection was independently associated with increased mortality, but the association varied by viral etiology, with influenza showing the strongest link.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings suggest that monitoring for Aspergillus in patients with viral pneumonia, particularly influenza, may be important for risk assessment and clinical management.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is retrospective and may be subject to biases, and the association between Aspergillus and mortality varied by virus type, indicating potential confounding factors.

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在调查病毒性肺炎患者下呼吸道曲霉检测与 死亡率 之间的关联,强调了解病毒性肺炎背景下真菌合并感染的必要性。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 这项回顾性多中心 队列研究 研究纳入了中国 929 名住院的病毒性肺炎患者,重点关注具有不同病毒病因的患者,包括流感、SARS-CoV-2 和其他病毒。
analysis_zh.methods: 暴露定义为使用培养、实时 PCR 或宏基因组下一代测序进行下呼吸道曲霉菌检测。使用 R 版本 3.6.3 和 Free Statistics 版本 2.2 进行统计分析。
analysis_zh.main_results: 929 名患者中,有 175 名患者检出曲霉菌(18.8%),其中流感组检出率最高(33.2%),其次是 SARS-CoV-2(14.6%)和其他病毒(7.4%)(P < 0.001)。与其他病毒组(4.2%,P = 0.004)相比,SARS-CoV-2 组(17.5%)和流感组(16.8%)的住院 死亡率 显着较高。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究发现,曲霉菌检测与 死亡率 增加独立相关,但这种关联因病毒病因而异,其中流感的关联性最强。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现表明,监测病毒性肺炎(尤其是流感)患者的曲霉菌可能对风险评估和临床管理很重要。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究是回顾性的,可能存在偏差,曲霉菌和 死亡率 之间的关联因病毒类型而异,表明存在潜在的混杂因素。

papers.full_text: BackgroundCOVID-19-related non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) disrupted the circulation of many respiratory pathogens. After these measures were lifted, pediatric respiratory pathogen activity may have changed in pathogen-specific ways. However, laboratory-based evidence using continuous multi-year data, interrupted time-series analysis, and contextual factors such as meteorology, air quality, and school calendars remains limited.MethodsWe conducted a single-center retrospective laboratory study of pediatric and neonatal inpatients aged 0–14 years with clinically diagnosed lower respiratory tract infection from January 2021 to December 2025. After 7-day deduplication within the same child, 20,250 throat-swab testing records were included. The NPI period was January 2021–December 2022, and the post-NPI period was January 2023–December 2025. Thirteen pathogen categories were analyzed using period comparisons, interrupted time-series models, and multivariable logistic regression incorporating meteorological factors, air quality index, and school-term status.ResultsOverall positivity was higher in the post-NPI period than in the NPI period (75.4% vs. 58.8%), and co-detection was also higher in the post-NPI period (15.2% vs. 6.0%). Pathogen-specific interrupted time-series analysis showed heterogeneous patterns: human adenovirus showed a robust immediate level decrease (−13.00 percentage points; 95% CI, −20.13 to −5.87; FDR-adjusted P = 0.005), whereas human rhinovirus showed a significant positive trend change after the January 2023 interruption (+1.07 percentage points per month; 95% CI, 0.63–1.50; FDR-adjusted P < 0.001), with a positive post-NPI slope (+0.64 percentage points per month). Higher temperature was associated with lower positivity of human respiratory syncytial virus, influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus, and influenza B virus, but higher positivity of human parainfluenza virus and human bocavirus. School-term status was associated with higher human rhinovirus positivity (aOR, 1.84; 95% CI, 1.34–2.52; FDR-adjusted P = 0.002).ConclusionThe NPI and post-NPI periods showed distinct and heterogeneous temporal patterns in pediatric respiratory pathogen detection. These findings support integrated hospital-based laboratory surveillance centered on pathogen-specific temporal trends and interpreted alongside demographic, multi-pathogen, environmental, school-calendar, and longer-term temporal context. 2Materials and methods2.1Study design, setting, and data sourceThis single-center, laboratory-based retrospective observational study was conducted in the Department of Clinical Laboratory at Beijing Anzhen Nanchong Hospital of Capital Medical University and Nanchong Central Hospital, located in Nanchong, Sichuan Province, China. The hospital is a tertiary general hospital and clinical teaching hospital that receives patients from Nanchong and surrounding areas. Pediatric respiratory pathogen nucleic acid testing records from January 1, 2021, to December 31, 2025, were extracted from the laboratory information system. Throughout the study period, the data-collecting hospital, clinical laboratory, and respiratory pathogen testing framework remained consistent. Annual pediatric and neonatal inpatient volumes from 2021 to 2025 were obtained from hospital administrative records and used to calculate the number of respiratory pathogen testing records per 100 inpatient admissions as a contextual measure of testing volume across study periods.2.2Study populationEligible testing records were from pediatric or neonatal inpatients aged 0–14 years with a clinician-recorded diagnosis of lower respiratory tract infection on the laboratory test request. These patients underwent routine 13-target multiplex respiratory pathogen testing between January 1, 2021, and December 31, 2025. Testing was ordered by clinicians according to the child's clinical presentation and diagnostic needs. Throat swabs were collected for respiratory pathogen nucleic acid testing. Records were required to contain complete information on sex, age, application date, and pathogen detection results. Outpatient and emergency department records were not included. Throughout the study period, the source wards, age range, eligibility criteria, and specimen type remained consistent.A total of 21,132 original identification records were initially available. After preliminary data cleaning, variable harmonization, and verification of key fields, 20,296 preliminary testing records were retained. To reduce the influence of repeated short-term testing from the same child, 7-day deduplication was performed using medical record numbers. For each child, testing records were ordered chronologically by application time; when multiple respiratory pathogen tests occurred within a 7-day window, only the first record was retained, whereas a test performed more than 7 days after the previously retained record was considered a new testing event. After deduplication, 46 short-term duplicate records were removed, leaving 20,250 testing records for the main analysis, including 6,490 records from the NPI period and 13,760 from the post-NPI period. The final dataset covered 60 consecutive months from January 2021 to December 2025. The overall study design, data-cleaning process, 7-day deduplication procedure, study-period classification, and analytical workflow are summarized in Figure 1.Figure 1Study design, data cleaning, and analytical workflow. The figure shows the data source, exclusion process, 7-day deduplication, study-period classification, and analytical framework. The NPI period was defined as January 2021 to December 2022, and the post-NPI period was defined as January 2023 to December 2025. During 7-day deduplication, only the first testing record from the same child within a 7-day window was retained. NPI, non-pharmaceutical intervention.Flowchart of study record selection and analysis. A total of 21,132 pediatric 13-pathogen respiratory nucleic acid testing records were screened; 836 records were excluded during data cleaning, leaving 20,296 preliminary records. After excluding 46 non-first repeat tests within 7 days, 20,250 records remained. These were classified into the NPI period (January 2021-December 2022; n = 6,490) and post-NPI period (January 2023–December 2025; n = 13,760), followed by risk-ratio, interrupted time-series, multivariable, age-stratified, co-detection, and sensitivity analyses.Children were categorized into four age groups: <1, 1–<3, 3–<6, and 6–14 years. This age stratification was selected according to commonly used pediatric respiratory infection epidemiology and the social contact patterns of children in China, broadly corresponding to infancy, early childhood mainly under home care, kindergarten age, and school age.2.3Respiratory pathogen testing and pathogen definitionsRespiratory pathogen nucleic acid testing was performed using a multiplex detection kit for 13 respiratory pathogens based on fluorescence PCR followed by capillary electrophoresis (PN: 1060071; Health GeneTech Co., Ltd., Ningbo, China). Nucleic acid extraction was performed using a TANBead SLA-32 automated nucleic acid extraction system. PCR amplification was performed using a SLAN-96P real-time PCR system. Amplification products were detected using an Applied Biosystems 3500 Dx Genetic Analyzer for capillary electrophoresis-based detection and fragment analysis. Sample processing, nucleic acid extraction, PCR amplification, capillary electrophoresis, quality control, and result interpretation were performed according to the manufacturer's instructions and local standard operating procedures.The main analysis included 13 respiratory pathogen categories: influenza A virus not further classified by this panel (InfA-NFC), influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus, seasonal influenza A (H3N2) virus, influenza B virus, human respiratory syncytial virus, human parainfluenza virus, human metapneumovirus, human rhinovirus, human adenovirus, seasonal human coronaviruses, human bocavirus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and Chlamydia spp. In this study, InfA-NFC referred to records positive for the manufacturer-reported generic influenza A target, listed as InfA in the manufacturer's instructions, but not classified as influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus or seasonal influenza A (H3N2) virus. The seasonal human coronaviruses category did not include SARS-CoV-2. Throughout the study period, SARS-CoV-2 testing, when clinically indicated, was performed through a separate dedicated nucleic acid testing pathway and was therefore not included in the fixed 13-target respiratory pathogen panel analyzed in this study. The Chlamydia category was not further differentiated into C. trachomatis or C. pneumoniae. Pathogen abbreviations, full pathogen names, manufacturer-reported detection targets, and limits of detection are provided in Supplementary Table S1.A composite influenza A variable was defined as positivity for any influenza A-related analytic category, including InfA-NFC, influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus, or seasonal influenza A(H3N2) virus. This composite variable was used only for descriptive summaries and was not included as an additional category in the main risk ratio, multiple-comparison, interrupted time-series, or multivariable regression analyses to avoid double counting. Overall positivity was defined as positivity for at least one of the 13 main respiratory pathogen categories. Co-detection was defined as positivity for two or more of the 13 main pathogen categories in the same testing record. Positivity and co-detection rates were calculated using the corresponding number of testing records as the denominator. A 13-target-negative record was defined as a testing record in which none of the 13 main respiratory pathogen categories was detected. Overall positivity and 13-target-negative proportions describe laboratory detection among tested pediatric and neonatal inpatients and were not intended as estimates of community incidence or prevalence.2.4Study periods, seasons, and school-term statusThe study period was divided according to the timing of COVID-19 policy adjustment in China and the monthly structure of the dataset. January 2021 to December 2022 was defined as the NPI period, and January 2023 to December 2025 was defined as the post-NPI period. In interrupted time-series analyses, January 2023 was treated as the first post-intervention month. Seasons were defined by calendar month: spring, March to May; summer, June to August; autumn, September to November; and winter, December to February. School-term status was defined at the calendar-day level according to the official local school calendar rather than by calendar month alone and assigned to each testing record based on the application date. Each testing record was classified as occurring during an in-school term or a vacation period. This variable was used as a population-level contextual indicator of periods with increased or decreased community contact networks related to kindergarten and school attendance.2.5Meteorological and air-quality dataDaily meteorological observations for Nanchong, Sichuan Province, China were obtained from RP5 (Reliable Prognosis), a publicly available weather data platform providing observational data from ground weather stations. Daily air quality index (AQI) records were obtained from the 2345 Weather historical weather database for Nanchong, a publicly accessible weather and air-quality information platform that provides city-level historical weather records with daily air-quality information (https://tianqi.2345.com/wea_history/57411.htm; accessed July 4, 2026). Before monthly aggregation, extracted AQI records were checked for completeness, date consistency, plausible value ranges, and temporal continuity. Daily temperature, relative humidity, and AQI records were aggregated into monthly means for each calendar month and linked to individual testing records by year-month. Temperature was modeled per 1 °C increase, relative humidity per 10% increase, and AQI per 10-unit increase. Meteorological and AQI variables were available for all 60 calendar months from January 2021 to December 2025 and were matched to the testing dataset by year-month.2.6Statistical analysisAll statistical analyses were based on the final analytic dataset of 20,250 testing records. Categorical variables were summarized as counts and percentages. Continuous variables were summarized as medians with interquartile ranges or means with standard deviations, as appropriate. All tests were two-sided, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. For multiple comparisons across the 13 main pathogen categories, the Benjamini–Hochberg method was used to control the false discovery rate (FDR). All statistical analyses were performed using Python software. Data management and aggregation were conducted using pandas and NumPy. Statistical calculations and modeling were performed using SciPy and statsmodels, and figures were generated using matplotlib.2.6.1Baseline characteristics and period comparisonsBaseline characteristics and pathogen detection profiles were compared between the NPI and post-NPI periods. Categorical variables were compared using the χ2 test or Fisher's exact test, as appropriate. Continuous variables were compared using the Mann–Whitney U test or t test, depending on distributional characteristics. The composite influenza A variable was presented only as a descriptive summary, with influenza A subtypes listed separately. Continuous age is presented as median (interquartile range) and was compared between the NPI and post-NPI periods using the Mann–Whitney U test.2.6.2Risk ratio analysisDetection risks for the 13 main respiratory pathogen categories were compared between the NPI and post-NPI periods. For each pathogen, positivity rates were calculated for both periods, and risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated. FDR-adjusted P values were used to assess statistical robustness under multiple testing. As an additional RSV-focused supplementary analysis, age was reclassified into clinically relevant categories for RSV burden and prevention strategies. RSV detection was first compared between children aged <2 years and those aged ≥2 years. Children were further categorized as 0–<6 months, 6–<12 months, 12–<24 months, and ≥24 months. For each category, RSV positivity was summarized for the NPI and post-NPI periods, and post-NPI vs. NPI risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), P values, and FDR-adjusted P values were calculated. This RSV-specific supplementary analysis was designed to provide clinical and public-health detail for the age windows most relevant to infant and toddler RSV prevention.2.6.3Interrupted time-series analysisTo evaluate whether the period difference in overall positivity could reflect a general long-term trend, monthly overall positivity was first analyzed using a single time-trend model without an interruption term. A segmented interrupted time-series model was then fitted using January 2023 as the first post-interruption month, corresponding to the January 8, 2023 policy transition, to estimate the pre-interruption trend, immediate level change, and post-interruption trend change. A joint Wald test evaluated the combined evidence for the immediate level and trend changes, and a grouped binomial model based on monthly positive and negative counts was used as a sensitivity analysis.Interrupted time-series (ITS) segmented regression models were used to assess immediate level changes and post-intervention trend changes in monthly pathogen positivity after the lifting of NPIs. ITS and segmented regression models are commonly used to evaluate level and slope changes after public health policy or intervention changes (21–24).For each pathogen, the monthly positivity rate was used as the outcome. The core independent variables included time, intervention status, and time after intervention. Month fixed effects were included to account for seasonality. Models were weighted by the monthly number of testing records. Newey–West robust standard errors were used to account for potential autocorrelation (25). The primary model used Newey–West lag = 1, and lag = 3 was used as a sensitivity analysis.The model was specified as: Yt = β0 + β1 × time + β2 × intervention + β3 × post-intervention time + month fixed effects + εt, where β1 represents the pre-intervention monthly trend, β2 represents the immediate level change after the lifting of NPIs, and β3 represents the post-intervention trend change.2.6.4Multivariable logistic regressionTo evaluate factors associated with pathogen positivity, separate multivariable logistic regression models were fitted for each of the 13 main respiratory pathogen categories. The core independent variables were monthly mean temperature, monthly mean relative humidity, monthly mean AQI, and school-term status. Models were adjusted for age group, sex, and pandemic phase. Because meteorological exposures, seasonality, and time trends may be correlated, season was not included in the primary model to reduce potential collinearity; this approach was consistent with general considerations in environmental time-series modeling (26). Cluster-robust standard errors were estimated at the year-month level. Results were reported as adjusted odds ratios (aORs) with 95% CIs. To assess whether environmental and temporal associations differed between the NPI and post-NPI periods, separate interaction models were fitted by adding temperature × phase, relative humidity × phase, AQI × phase, and school term × phase terms to the pathogen-specific multivariable models. Across 13 pathogen categories and four contextual factors, 52 interaction tests were prespecified. School-term status was associated with higher human rhinovirus positivity (aOR, 1.84; 95% CI, 1.34–2.52; FDR-adjusted P = 0.002).ConclusionThe NPI and post-NPI periods showed distinct and heterogeneous temporal patterns in pediatric respiratory pathogen detection. These findings support integrated hospital-based laboratory surveillance centered on pathogen-specific temporal trends and interpreted alongside demographic, multi-pathogen, environmental, school-calendar, and longer-term temporal context.
full_text_sections.methods: 2Materials and methods2.1Study design, setting, and data sourceThis single-center, laboratory-based retrospective observational study was conducted in the Department of Clinical Laboratory at Beijing Anzhen Nanchong Hospital of Capital Medical University and Nanchong Central Hospital, located in Nanchong, Sichuan Province, China. The hospital is a tertiary general hospital and clinical teaching hospital that receives patients from Nanchong and surrounding areas. Pediatric respiratory pathogen nucleic acid testing records from January 1, 2021, to December 31, 2025, were extracted from the laboratory information system. Throughout the study period, the data-collecting hospital, clinical laboratory, and respiratory pathogen testing framework remained consistent. Annual pediatric and neonatal inpatient volumes from 2021 to 2025 were obtained from hospital administrative records and used to calculate the number of respiratory pathogen testing records per 100 inpatient admissions as a contextual measure of testing volume across study periods.2.2Study populationEligible testing records were from pediatric or neonatal inpatients aged 0–14 years with a clinician-recorded diagnosis of lower respiratory tract infection on the laboratory test request. These patients underwent routine 13-target multiplex respiratory pathogen testing between January 1, 2021, and December 31, 2025. Testing was ordered by clinicians according to the child's clinical presentation and diagnostic needs. Throat swabs were collected for respiratory pathogen nucleic acid testing. Records were required to contain complete information on sex, age, application date, and pathogen detection results. Outpatient and emergency department records were not included. Throughout the study period, the source wards, age range, eligibility criteria, and specimen type remained consistent.A total of 21,132 original identification records were initially available. After preliminary data cleaning, variable harmonization, and verification of key fields, 20,296 preliminary testing records were retained. To reduce the influence of repeated short-term testing from the same child, 7-day deduplication was performed using medical record numbers. For each child, testing records were ordered chronologically by application time; when multiple respiratory pathogen tests occurred within a 7-day window, only the first record was retained, whereas a test performed more than 7 days after the previously retained record was considered a new testing event. After deduplication, 46 short-term duplicate records were removed, leaving 20,250 testing records for the main analysis, including 6,490 records from the NPI period and 13,760 from the post-NPI period. The final dataset covered 60 consecutive months from January 2021 to December 2025. The figure shows the data source, exclusion process, 7-day deduplication, study-period classification, and analytical framework. The NPI period was defined as January 2021 to December 2022, and the post-NPI period was defined as January 2023 to December 2025. During 7-day deduplication, only the first testing record from the same child within a 7-day window was retained. A total of 21,132 pediatric 13-pathogen respiratory nucleic acid testing records were screened; 836 records were excluded during data cleaning, leaving 20,296 preliminary records. These were classified into the NPI period (January 2021-December 2022; n = 6,490) and post-NPI period (January 2023–December 2025; n = 13,760), followed by risk-ratio, interrupted time-series, multivariable, age-stratified, co-detection, and sensitivity analyses.Children were categorized into four age groups: <1, 1–<3, 3–<6, and 6–14 years. This age stratification was selected according to commonly used pediatric respiratory infection epidemiology and the social contact patterns of children in China, broadly corresponding to infancy, early childhood mainly under home care, kindergarten age, and school age.2.3Respiratory pathogen testing and pathogen definitionsRespiratory pathogen nucleic acid testing was performed using a multiplex detection kit for 13 respiratory pathogens based on fluorescence PCR followed by capillary electrophoresis (PN: 1060071; Health GeneTech Co., Ltd., Ningbo, China). Nucleic acid extraction was performed using a TANBead SLA-32 automated nucleic acid extraction system. PCR amplification was performed using a SLAN-96P real-time PCR system. The seasonal human coronaviruses category did not include SARS-CoV-2. Throughout the study period, SARS-CoV-2 testing, when clinically indicated, was performed through a separate dedicated nucleic acid testing pathway and was therefore not included in the fixed 13-target respiratory pathogen panel analyzed in this study. The Chlamydia category was not further differentiated into C. trachomatis or C. pneumoniae. This composite variable was used only for descriptive summaries and was not included as an additional category in the main risk ratio, multiple-comparison, interrupted time-series, or multivariable regression analyses to avoid double counting. Overall positivity was defined as positivity for at least one of the 13 main respiratory pathogen categories. Co-detection was defined as positivity for two or more of the 13 main pathogen categories in the same testing record. Positivity and co-detection rates were calculated using the corresponding number of testing records as the denominator. A 13-target-negative record was defined as a testing record in which none of the 13 main respiratory pathogen categories was detected. Overall positivity and 13-target-negative proportions describe laboratory detection among tested pediatric and neonatal inpatients and were not intended as estimates of community incidence or prevalence.2.4Study periods, seasons, and school-term statusThe study period was divided according to the timing of COVID-19 policy adjustment in China and the monthly structure of the dataset.
